chapter: Europe and the Black and Blue years
title: The 1972-73 Black and Blue session with Jay McShann and Milt Buckner
summary: After the Basie tribute Stanley Dance arranged, she was in France five days later, touring for Monestier and recording 'Helen Comes Back' with Jay McShann and Milt Buckner. Dance praises McShann's range beyond blues piano.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: That was probably when you first met Dr. Chavron.
Yes, it was.
Well, tell me about that because you know, Monestier does such a great job and people here don't know anything about it, and he gets all the good musicians and he tours everybody.
Yes. Well, I didn't know anything about him until then. You know, when I came over and Stanley (Dance) came and had me do this Basie thing in '72.
Yes, at Newport.
And five days later I was in France.
And also, you made that record.
Yeah, that was a Black and Blue.
And were you on the road for him for about two weeks?
Yeah, let's see, I did three concerts, --you know I don't do any one-nighters-- three or four and then I made my recordings.
Yeah.
And I've got that record here.
I've got it too but I'd like to look at it. Maybe we could even refresh our memories because

S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC.
WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
I wanted to ask you who was on that record.
Jay McShann and Milt Buckner.
That's right. Stanley was saying to me last night, what did Helen have to say about Jay and Milt.
Oh well, I got everything good to say about them. The singing is getting better, and better and better.
That's a fact. And he's at last getting better known. He goes more places. He certainly deserves it, doesn't he?
Yeah.

You know Helen, something Stanleyand I have always done, noticed about Jay. People think he's a blue pianist. He's alot more than a blues pianist. You know, if you noticed, and you'd notice more than I, there's alot of very pretty things. And I think one of the reasons is, when he went back to Kansas City to study at the Conservatory.
I'm glad he did that.
So you hear those little things in his work which you wouldn't expect from a blues pianist. Of course Milt Buckner livens up things.
